name: Ananthapura Lake Temple (Sri Ananthapadmanabha Swamy)
tagline: Kerala’s only lake temple — traditional moolasthanam of Padmanabhaswamy
summary: A unique 9th‑century lake shrine at Ananthapura, traditionally held as the moolasthanam of Sree Padmanabhaswamy; famed for carved wooden panels, Navagraha painting and the temple crocodile lore.
description: Ananthapura Lake Temple stands on a small island at the centre of a spring‑fed rectangular tank in the village of Ananthapura (near Kumbla) and is the only temple built in a lake in Kerala. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

Local tradition holds that this shrine is the moolasthanam (original abode) of Ananthapadmanabha — the same tutelary form of Vishnu worshipped at Sree Padmanabhaswamy, Thiruvananthapuram — a claim told in legend though not firmly dated by documentary evidence. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ananthapura_Lake_Temple))

Visitors find an intimate temple reached by a single footbridge, a namaskara mandapam with richly carved wooden ceilings showing Dashavatara scenes, Navagraha paintings in the muktha‑mandapam and a small cave at the lake’s edge linked to the origin legend. The site blends architectural interest with layered ritual and astrological associations. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))
highlights: Kerala’s only temple built in the middle of a lake
Traditionally regarded as the moolasthanam of Padmanabhaswamy
Fine carved wooden Dashavatara panels on mandapam ceilings
Navagraha (nine planets) painting and astrological motifs
Longstanding crocodile guardian lore (Babiya and successors)

sections.heading: Background
body: The present shrine is traditionally dated to the early medieval period (often cited as the 9th century in guide sources), though scholars stress the historical picture is uncertain and much of the origin story survives as legend. The place is important for its unique site — a sanctum sitting in the lake reached by a single footbridge — and for the surviving wooden carving programme. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

sections.heading: Ritual lore and astrological associations
body: Local ritual lore connects Ananthapura to Vilwamangalam Swamiyar and to the journey of the Anantha Padmanabha deity toward Thiruvananthapuram; this is presented as a traditional moolasthanam claim rather than as proven history. Some modern guides and scholarship recommend presenting the moolasthanam as tradition when interpreting the site. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

The temple interior displays Navagraha (nine‑planet) paintings in the muktha‑mandapam and the carved Dashavatara panels, features that draw devotees for both devotional and astrological observances; these iconographic elements make the shrine a local focus for planetary remedies and observances tied to Vaishnava practice. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

Ananthapura’s lake also carries a long communal story about a crocodile guardian. The famous crocodile ‘Babiya’ died on 2022‑10‑09; local reports record a new crocodile appearing in the lake in November 2023, a development that devotees treated as a continuing lineage of the guardian. These events figure in ritual memory and pilgrimage narratives. ([thenewsminute.com](https://www.thenewsminute.com/article/babiya-kerala-s-vegetarian-crocodile-dies-ananthapura-temple-pond-168727?utm_source=openai))

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Walk the narrow footbridge to the namaskara mandapam and study the carved wooden ceilings (Dashavatara scenes) and painted Navagraha panel in the muktha‑mandapam — these are the site’s artistic highlights. Allow time to view the lake, the cave opening at the northeast corner and the lakeside shrines. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

Observe puja and offerings, and (with respect) note the crocodile’s usual resting spots near the cave mouth; devotees sometimes view the animal as a temple guardian and an element in ritual practice. Photography and access inside the sanctum can be restricted — confirm on arrival. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Temple timings reported by tourism sources are typically early morning and evening (for example 05:30–12:30 and 17:30–19:30), but local practice can vary; confirm the current schedule with the temple office before you travel. The site is 4–6 km from Kumbla; the nearest major station is Kumbla (about 5 km) and the nearest airport is Mangalore International Airport (approx. 52–54 km). ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

The temple holds its annual Varshika Mahotsavam in the Malayalam month of Kumbham (roughly February–March) with cultural programmes, bhajana and a ceremonial procession across the lake; that festival is the busiest time to visit. Confirm festival dates each year. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/1000festivals/assets/uploads/pdf/1507657854-0.pdf))

latest.text: Roampedia publishes a careful, updated guide that presents the moolasthanam claim as local tradition and emphasises the site’s independent significance; the piece is useful for readers who want a cautious, source‑aware account.
Devotees and local media report a new crocodile appearing in the temple lake about a year after the death of the famous crocodile Babiya.
Babiya, the temple’s long‑lived and much‑revered ‘vegetarian’ crocodile, dies; the event received national media coverage and a ceremonial burial at the shrine.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March (pleasant weather); festival crowds peak in Kumbham (Feb–Mar).
visitorInfo.howToReach: By rail: Kumbla station (~5 km). By air: Mangalore International Airport (~52–54 km). By road: follow Kumbla–Badiyadka/Naikap roads and take the turn to Ananthapura; the shrine sits on a lake reached by a short footbridge. Confirm last‑mile conditions locally. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ananthapura_Lake_Temple))
etiquette: Present the moolasthanam story as local tradition rather than proven history; the site is best enjoyed on its own aesthetic and ritual terms. ([roampedia.com](https://roampedia.com/india/kerala/kasaragod/kumbla-and-ananthapura/guides/ananthapura-the-past-is-obscure-and-that-is-the-honest-sentence))

Dress modestly and follow temple etiquette; check puja times and photography rules with the temple before entering the sanctum. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/destination/ananthapura-lake-temple-kasaragod/159/))

Carry water and footwear suitable for short uneven paths; parking and visitor facilities are basic — confirm availability if you travel by car. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/1000festivals/assets/uploads/pdf/1507657854-0.pdf))
